New Zealand closed the old portal for visitor visas. From 24th September only the new one

Immigration New Zealand is now accepting new applications for most visitor visas only through enhanced Immigration Online starting today. The old online platform for these categories no longer accepts new applications. The entry rules themselves have not changed. It's just the application channel that has changed.

This is not about visa-free entry or NZeTA. Those who already have the right to enter under electronic authorization are in a different queue. This is about the standard Visitor Visa: for tourism, business, medical treatment, parents and grandparents, and group visits. From 24th August, Group and Tour Escort visas also started using the new portal. From 24th September, the majority of other visitor categories will also transition to the new system.

There are two strict deadlines ahead. On 1st October, New Zealand will almost stop accepting paper applications for selected visitor and transit visas. After this date, paper applications will only be accepted in exceptional cases. On 8th October, the old forms will be completely phased out. Draft applications that were not submitted will be deleted. It's not archiving, but a complete reset. Applicants will need to start from scratch in the new portal and re-upload all documents.

Existing applications should not be affected. Unfinished draft applications in the old system can still be completed and submitted before 8th October. INZ promises to notify those with pending drafts. The categories "partner/child of a New Zealander" are still on the old platform for now. Partners and children of military personnel, students, or workers have already transitioned to the new system earlier, in June.

To access the new platform, you usually need a RealMe account. Then provide standard visa photos, documents, and translations in English, and pay online. The average processing time for a standard visitor visa is currently about a week, with most being processed within two weeks. Business visitor visas are processed faster: days, not weeks.

For travelers and tourists, the message is clear. Those who planned to "print out the form and take it to the visa center" are too late. Those who started an application in the old platform and abandoned it can either submit before 8th October or lose their progress. Those who are planning to visit should go straight to the new portal. The country has not closed its doors. It just stopped accepting applications through three different windows at the same time.

📌 Reentrancy: How a Smart Contract Can Open the Door to an Attack

Main Points
⏺ Reentrancy happens when a contract gives control to an external contract too early
⏺ An attacker can call the function again before balances are updated
⏺ This post explains why execution order can decide the safety of funds

1️⃣ Core Idea — a contract sends funds or calls another contract, and that contract jumps back into the original function.
2️⃣ The Problem — if the user balance is reduced after sending funds, the attacker may withdraw multiple times.
3️⃣ Why It’s Dangerous — the contract “thinks” funds are still available even though withdrawal already started.
4️⃣ Common Defense — update state first, send funds after, and use protective locks.
5️⃣ Practical Check — if a protocol handles withdrawals, external calls, and complex logic, audits matter a lot.

Final Thoughts

Reentrancy is an attack on execution order. Sometimes the bug is not what the contract does, but when it does it.

Here's a small fact about Python 🐍

The := operator is called the "walrus" because the symbols resemble the eyes and tusks of a walrus 🦭

It was introduced in Python 3.8 and allows you to assign a value to a variable and use it directly within the expression at the same time.

For example:

while (line := input("Say something: ")) != "quit":
    print(f"You said: {line}")

Without it, you would have to retrieve the value separately using input(), and then check it.

Have you ever used the := operator in your code?

The Corporate Prosecutor

OpenAI says it catches foreign influence operations. Conveniently, it owns the machine they allegedly used, the logs that identify them, the rules that define abuse and the blog where the verdict appears.

When the company says it disrupted a Chinese, Russian, Iranian or Israeli network, the public gets a polished dossier: operation names, selected prompts, a sample of output and a geopolitical label. 

What stays inside OpenAI is the evidence that would let anyone test the label: account logs, clustering rules, false-positive rates, alternative explanations and internal dissent.

A platform can ban users from its own product. “This account used our model to write text” is a fact about the platform. 

“We uncovered a state-linked influence operation” is a claim about coordination, intent and political purpose. 

That claim reaches governments, reporters and researchers without an adversarial process, because the only witness with full access is also the prosecutor.

The business model completes the loop. Generative AI makes phishing, malware, multilingual propaganda and synthetic personas cheaper to produce. 

The same companies sell the filters, monitoring and attribution meant to contain them. The more dangerous the information environment becomes, the more indispensable its landlord appears.

OpenAI’s reports may be right. That is not the standard. A private company should not get to turn an internal moderation judgment into geopolitical fact while keeping the underlying record private.
